claims.text: Integrating chain-of-thought prompting with few-shot learning increases automated scoring accuracy in large language models.
Combining human-labeled data with LLM-generated synthetic data in semi-supervised learning improves the scoring accuracy of mathematical self-explanations.
Large language models in automated grading risk perpetuating biases present in their training datasets.
Large language models can produce plausible yet incorrect or misaligned responses (hallucinations) during automated evaluation.
Traditional manual grading systems suffer from scalability limitations due to time and labor constraints in large classes.

evidence.description: Implementation of Chain-of-Thought (CoT) with few-shot learning resulted in increased scoring accuracy in GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 models on science assessments.
Integrating human-labeled and synthetic data generated by an LLM in a semi-supervised method significantly improved the accuracy of assessing mathematical self-explanations.
Biases in training data can result in unfair grading, particularly affecting minority student groups or nonstandard language users.
LLMs are prone to generating plausible yet incorrect or misaligned responses, known as hallucinations, which pose significant challenges in educational settings.
Manual grading is inherently time-consuming and requires substantial human effort, leading to feedback delays in growing class sizes.

methodologies.name: Literature review and case study synthesis of LLM-based grading practices
methodologies.description: Qualitative synthesis and thematic evaluation of existing literature and case studies regarding large language model integration into educational assessment and grading.

limitations.text: Traditional manual grading methods lack scalability and face delays in feedback provision in large-scale courses.
Manual grading is subject to subjective evaluator biases and consistency variations across different instructors or over time.
Large language models present risks of hallucination and black-box opacity in automated grading decisions.
LLMs trained predominantly on native English data may produce biased evaluations for non-native English speakers or nonstandard language users.

future_work.text: Enhancing LLMs to understand cognitive patterns for personalized educational interventions and integrating multimodal inputs for comprehensive assessment.
Developing techniques to improve the interpretability and explainability of LLM-based grading decisions to build educator trust.
Addressing ethical concerns, algorithmic bias, and hallucinations in LLMs through regular dataset audits and human-in-the-loop oversight.
